episode_title: Risk and Regression: Basic Linear Regression — Episode 1 of 2

scenes.dialogue: This chapter deliberately restricts regression to one explanatory variable. That may sound narrow, but the source says most deep regression ideas can be developed there with simple algebra and two-dimensional graphics. Our goal is to use that simplicity as a laboratory: see the relationship, fit it, measure its uncertainty, and challenge the model when the data disagree. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The source’s first running example follows average lottery sales across fifty randomly selected Wisconsin ZIP-code areas over forty weeks, from April 1998 through January 1999. The response is SALES and the initial explanatory variable is population, POP. Tickets are generally one dollar, so ticket count equals lottery revenue. The first intuition is simple: more people should mean more sales. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Before relating variables, the chapter asks us to understand each one alone. POP has mean 9,311, median 4,406, standard deviation 11,098, minimum 280, and maximum 39,098. SALES has mean 6,495, median 2,426, standard deviation 8,103, minimum 189, and maximum 33,181. Both histograms are right-skewed, with many small areas and relatively few large areas. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

A data point is an ordered pair, x_i and y_i. For the first lottery area, the source gives population x_1=435 and sales y_1=1,285.4. The complete sample is the sequence of fifty such pairs. This notation matters because regression makes its general statements one observation at a time before combining all observations into a fitted relationship. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Once each variable is summarized alone, the scatterplot becomes the basic graphical tool for their relationship. Exact values may be lost in a plot, but the gain is a visual sense of direction and strength. For the lottery data, the plotted ZIP codes suggest that larger populations tend to produce more lottery revenue. That is a starting clue, not the end of analysis. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The ordinary Pearson correlation r standardizes both variables and averages their cross-products. Its range is always from minus one to one. Positive values indicate positive correlation, negative values indicate negative correlation, and larger absolute values indicate a stronger linear relationship. At r=1 or r=-1, every point lies exactly on a straight line with the relevant direction. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Correlation is location and scale invariant. Adding one hundred dollars to every sales figure changes the mean but not deviations from the mean. Dividing population by one thousand changes its units, but standardized values remain unchanged. That is why r is dimensionless and can be compared across datasets. It also explains why correlation describes linear shape rather than raw units. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The chapter’s classic warning is y=x squared. Using the symmetric x values minus two, minus one, zero, one, two, the relationship is perfect but r=0. Positive and negative contributions cancel. So a zero correlation does not mean no relationship; it means no linear relationship. A scatterplot remains indispensable because numerical summaries alone can miss visible structure. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

For the lottery data, the source reports r=0.886 for SALES and POP. That is close to one, so the chapter calls it a strong positive correlation. It tells us population can help anticipate revenue, but it has not yet given us a concrete prediction rule. For that we need a line, and the chapter chooses a line by the method of least squares. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Drawing a line by eye is not a satisfactory scientific procedure. Different analysts can agree on the same points and draw different lines. Least squares supplies a reproducible rule. Begin with any candidate line y=b0 star plus b1 star x, measure each vertical deviation from the observed response, square it, and sum across observations. The least-squares line minimizes that sum. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The chapter solves the normal equations and gives the familiar results: b1 equals r times s_y over s_x, and b0 equals ybar minus b1 xbar. For the lottery sample, b1=0.647 and b0=469.7. The fitted regression line is yhat=469.7+0.647x. The hat reminds us this is a fitted estimate, not an observed sales amount. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Put x=10,000 into the lottery fitted line and you get 469.7 plus 0.647 times 10,000, or 6,939.7. This is the model’s point estimate of sales for a ZIP code with population 10,000. It is more tailored than simply predicting the overall sample mean of 6,495, because it uses information from the explanatory variable. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Regression can summarize simulated financial scenarios as well. The source discusses Manistre and Hancock’s simulation of a ten-year European put option, relating value-at-risk, VaR, to conditional tail expectation, CTE. They repeated simulations one thousand times, and the scatterplot between the two risk measures showed a strong but imperfect relationship, with r=0.782. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

A scatterplot, correlation, and fitted line summarize one dataset. To make claims about a broader population, the chapter introduces the basic linear regression model. Basic means one explanatory variable. In the observables representation, expected y_i equals beta0 plus beta1 x_i. The unknown beta parameters describe the population line, while b0 and b1 are sample estimates. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The basic model treats the observed x values as nonstochastic: inference about y is conditional on them. The chapter motivates this with stratified sampling, imagining each x value as a stratum. For example, one might study stock returns conditionally on firm asset size. It also cautions against selecting observations based on y, such as choosing the top fifty managers by return, because that is outcome-based selection. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Assumption F3 says the response variance is sigma squared for every observation. This common-variance assumption is called homoscedasticity. It says the vertical scatter around the population regression line does not systematically expand or contract as x changes. The chapter flags heteroscedasticity, varying variability by observation, as a model problem that will require more attention later. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The equivalent error representation writes y_i=beta0+beta1x_i+epsilon_i. Errors have mean zero, common variance sigma squared, and are independent. They gather the influence of unobserved variables affecting y. This representation is useful for goodness-of-fit calculations, but its weakness is practical: errors are unobserved, so their sampling basis cannot be directly verified. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

A fifth assumption often used is normality of the responses or errors. The chapter repeats the earlier point that exact normality is not necessary for many inference procedures because central limit theorems offer approximate normality. It can, however, matter for formal justification of procedures like t statistics. In visual terms, the model pictures responses scattered around a regression line, often by normal curves. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Section 2.3 asks whether the model is useful. Without x, ybar is a sensible estimate of each response, and Total SS is the sum of squared deviations from ybar. With x, each fitted value yhat_i becomes the estimate. The central decomposition says total deviation equals residual deviation plus explained deviation, and after squaring and summing: Total SS=Error SS+Regression SS. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The coefficient of determination R squared is Regression SS divided by Total SS: the proportion of variability explained by the regression line. It lies from zero to one. A perfect fitted line has Error SS zero and R squared one. A line that provides no response information has Regression SS zero and R squared zero. Larger values are better fits in this descriptive sense. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

Residuals are e_i=y_i-yhat_i. The mean square error is s squared=the sum of squared residuals divided by n-2, and s is its positive square root, the residual standard deviation. The n-2 denominator reflects two fitted coefficients. Least squares guarantees residuals average to zero. With this degrees-of-freedom adjustment, s squared is an unbiased estimator of sigma squared. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The lottery ANOVA table makes the bookkeeping visible. Regression SS is 2,527,165,015; Error SS is 690,116,755; Total SS is 3,217,281,770. The error degrees of freedom are 48 because n=50, and the error mean square is 14,377,432. The source reports R squared of 78.5 percent and a residual standard deviation near 3,792. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

The slope b1 is a weighted sum of responses. It is unbiased for beta1, and its variance is sigma squared divided by s_x squared times n-1. Replacing sigma with s gives se(b1)=s divided by s_x times the square root of n-1. More observations reduce it; tighter scatter around the line reduces it; a wider range of x values reduces it. These are practical design lessons. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.

That is our first pass through the model: relation, scatterplot, correlation, least squares, population assumptions, explained variation, residual variation, and slope precision. In the next episode we turn these quantities into inference, then test them through residual analysis, unusual observations, a financial CAPM application, software output, and matrix algebra. Keep the central distinction in mind: a fitted line is an estimate, not a guarantee. The practical takeaway is to connect the formula or graph to the data-generating question before treating it as a decision rule.
